A 4-year-old boy is brought to the clinic for a routine check-up.  The patient is feeling well, and he and his parents have no concerns.  On physical examination, an ejection sound and soft systolic murmur are noted at the upper sternal border.  Echocardiography is performed and a representative image of the short axis view at the aortic valve level is shown below.  Based on the observed abnormal findings, this patient is at greatest risk for which of the following?

explanation:
Bicuspid aortic valve

Epidemiology

  • Usually familial with autosomal dominant inheritance
  • Affects ~1% of population, more common in males
  • Strong association with Turner syndrome

Clinicalmanifestations

  • Accelerated valve calcification with early stenosis (eg, age ≥40)
  • Aortic regurgitation can develop (less common than stenosis)
  • Increased incidence of ascending aortic aneurysm

This patient has an ejection sound and systolic murmur at the upper sternal border, with echocardiography revealing a bicuspid aortic valve (BAV).  BAV is a common congenital heart defect found in approximately 1% of the general population; it results from fusion of 2 of the 3 normal aortic valve cusps, resulting in 2 functional valve leaflets.  The genetic mutations responsible for BAV can occur sporadically but are commonly inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.

The most common complication of BAV is early-onset aortic stenosis.  This complication occurs because BAV disrupts the hemodynamics surrounding the aortic valve and accelerates age-related valvular calcification (a process with pathophysiology similar to that of atherosclerosis).  Calcification of a BAV and development of severe aortic stenosis can occur as early as age 40, whereas calcification and severe aortic stenosis of a congenitally normal trileaflet aortic valve is rare prior to age 70.

Less commonly, BAV can disrupt valve closure and lead to aortic regurgitation (rather than stenosis) in relatively young adults.

(Choice A)  A patent foramen ovale (PFO) can allow for passage of a venous thromboembolism into the arterial circulation (paradoxical embolization) and is the most common cause of cryptogenic stroke.  PFO is present in up to a third of the general population, but it is not present with greater prevalence in patients with BAV.

(Choice C)  Eisenmenger syndrome develops when a left-to-right shunt (eg, ventricular septal defect) induces pulmonary arterial remodeling that eventually leads to shunt reversal (eg, right-to-left) with resultant hypoxemia and cyanosis.  BAV does not involve left-to-right shunting and does not increase risk for Eisenmenger syndrome.

(Choice D)  Episodic hypercyanotic spells (ie, tet episodes) are seen in patients with tetralogy of Fallot, often resulting from a dynamic increase in right ventricular outflow tract obstruction that facilitates right-to-left shunting through a large ventricular septal defect.  BAV does not cause cyanosis.

(Choice E)  Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is an inherited heart condition associated with an increased risk of sudden cardiac death during adolescence and early adulthood.  BAV does not substantially increase the risk of sudden cardiac death.

Educational objective:Early-onset aortic stenosis is the most common complication of a bicuspid aortic valve.  It results from disrupted hemodynamics and accelerated age-related valvular calcification, which can lead to severe aortic stenosis as early as age 40.  In comparison, age-related calcification of a congenitally normal trileaflet aortic valve rarely leads to severe aortic stenosis prior to age 70.​‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​​​​‌​​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌
